title: 2 Chronicles 29:1–11
context: Hezekiah begins to reign and, in his first month, opens and repairs the doors of the LORD’s house. He gathers the priests and Levites, calls them to sanctify themselves and the temple, confesses the unfaithfulness of the fathers, and announces his intent to make a covenant with the LORD. The parallel in 2 Kings 18:1-6 summarizes Hezekiah’s reform briefly, naming the removal of high places and the breaking of the bronze serpent; the temple cleansing described here appears only in Chronicles, which reports the removal of high places later (2 Chronicles 31:1) and does not mention the bronze serpent. Ahaz’s age at his accession and death and Hezekiah’s age at his own accession are difficult to reconcile, and interpreters suggest different reconstructions.

verses.text: Hezekiah began to reign when he was twenty-five years old, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Abijah, the daughter of Zechariah.
verses.arminianNotes: Hezekiah begins to reign at twenty-five and reigns twenty-nine years. Arminian readers see a new opportunity for Judah, and they note his mother’s name, Abijah, given as Abi in 2 Kings 18:2.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the figures match 2 Kings 18:2. If Ahaz reigned sixteen years from age twenty, the ages are hard to fit together, and interpreters propose co-regencies or other explanations.

verses.text: He did that which was right in the LORD’s eyes, according to all that David his father had done.
verses.arminianNotes: Hezekiah did right according to all that David had done. Arminian readers see a son choosing a path very different from his father’s, showing that family history does not determine faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the verdict matches 2 Kings 18:3, the highest praise given a king. As the Kings notes say, God’s grace raises a reformer from an unfaithful home.

verses.text: In the first year of his reign, in the first month, he opened the doors of the LORD’s house and repaired them.
verses.arminianNotes: In the first month of his first year he opened the doors of the LORD’s house and repaired them. Arminian readers see urgency: reform begins at once, reversing the closing of the doors by Ahaz (28:24).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this immediate action is described only in Chronicles; 2 Kings 18:4 begins with the high places and the bronze serpent. The Chronicler places the temple first.

verses.text: He brought in the priests and the Levites and gathered them together into the wide place on the east,
verses.arminianNotes: He brings the priests and Levites to the wide place on the east. Arminian readers see a king gathering those called to serve, so that renewal is shared rather than imposed by one man.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Hezekiah begins with the ministers of the sanctuary. The renewal of worship depends on those whom God had appointed to lead it.

verses.text: and said to them, “Listen to me, you Levites! Now sanctify yourselves, and sanctify the house of the LORD, the God of your fathers, and carry the filthiness out of the holy place.
verses.arminianNotes: Hezekiah calls the Levites to sanctify themselves and the house and to carry out the filthiness. Arminian readers see personal consecration as the starting point for any public renewal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the order of the command: first the ministers, then the house. The word filthiness names the defilement left by Ahaz’s reign in plain terms.

verses.text: For our fathers were unfaithful, and have done that which was evil in the LORD our God’s sight, and have forsaken him, and have turned away their faces from the habitation of the LORD, and turned their backs.
verses.arminianNotes: Hezekiah confesses that the fathers were unfaithful and turned their backs on the LORD’s habitation. Arminian readers see an honest admission of generational sin as the first step of repentance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the confession is specific: forsaking God and turning away from his dwelling. Hezekiah owns the nation’s history rather than excusing it.

verses.text: Also they have shut up the doors of the porch, and put out the lamps, and have not burned incense nor offered burnt offerings in the holy place to the God of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: The fathers shut the porch doors, put out the lamps, and stopped the incense and burnt offerings. Arminian readers see worship abandoned piece by piece, each neglect a choice to turn away.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the details correspond to the regular service required by the law (Exodus 27:20-21; 30:7-8). The neglect of these duties is presented as unfaithfulness to God himself.

verses.text: Therefore the LORD’s wrath was on Judah and Jerusalem, and he has delivered them to be tossed back and forth, to be an astonishment and a hissing, as you see with your eyes.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s wrath was on Judah, making it an astonishment and a hissing. Arminian readers see the king interpreting recent disasters as the consequences of the nation’s choices.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Hezekiah reading history through the covenant. The suffering the people had seen with their own eyes was God’s just response to their unfaithfulness.

verses.text: For behold, our fathers have fallen by the sword, and our sons and our daughters and our wives are in captivity for this.
verses.arminianNotes: Fathers have fallen by the sword, and sons, daughters, and wives are in captivity. Arminian readers note the human grief behind the theology, recalling the losses of 28:5-8.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the king connecting the captivity directly to the fathers’ sin. The grief is real, and it moves him toward covenant renewal rather than despair.

verses.text: Now it is in my heart to make a covenant with the LORD, the God of Israel, that his fierce anger may turn away from us.
verses.arminianNotes: It is in my heart to make a covenant with the LORD, that his fierce anger may turn away. Arminian readers see God genuinely responsive to repentance; the Jonah 3:10 box discusses such turning.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see covenant renewal as the God-given response to judgment. The king seeks reconciliation through the means God appointed, trusting that the LORD’s anger can be turned.

verses.text: My sons, don’t be negligent now; for the LORD has chosen you to stand before him, to minister to him, and that you should be his ministers and burn incense.”
verses.arminianNotes: Hezekiah urges the Levites not to be negligent, for the LORD has chosen them to minister. Arminian readers see a calling that must be embraced with diligence, not taken for granted.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the language of choosing, which grounds the Levites’ service in God’s appointment. Their privilege brings responsibility, and the king calls them to it as a father to sons.
